importance_detail.rationale: The bill proposes sweeping structural changes to the healthcare industry by prohibiting common ownership between pharmacies and pharmacy benefit managers or insurers, requiring widespread divestitures, and establishing new private and public enforcement mechanisms.

label: H.R. 8779

latest_action.text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini.

summary: H.R. 8779, known as the Patients Before Monopolies Act or the PBM Act, prohibits any entity from maintaining common ownership of both a pharmacy and an insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager (PBM). It requires companies that currently share such ownership to divest their pharmacy businesses within one year, provides enforcement mechanisms for federal and state authorities as well as private citizens, and grants antitrust agencies oversight and rulemaking powers.

affected_groups.effect: Must divest any owned or controlled pharmacies within one year or face profit escrow, oversight by a divestiture trustee, and civil enforcement actions.
affected_groups.group: Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) and Insurance Companies

affected_groups.effect: Must separate structurally from any parent companies that operate as health insurers or pharmacy benefit managers.
Gain a private right of action to sue for damages resulting from violations, with potential recovery of treble damages and legal costs.
Gain expanded jurisdiction, enforcement authority, review powers, and the ability to bring civil actions against violators.
affected_groups.group: Federal Agencies (FTC, DOJ) and State Attorneys General

key_provisions: Makes it unlawful for any person or entity to directly or indirectly own or control both a pharmacy and an insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager.
Requires any person violating the ownership prohibition to fully divest the pharmacy within one year of the Act's enactment.

Authorizes the FTC and the Assistant Attorney General for the Antitrust Division to jointly or separately enforce the divestment rules, issue milestone guidance, and place 10 percent of non-compliant profits into escrow.

Allows federal inspectors general, the DOJ, the FTC, and state attorneys general to bring civil actions, and establishes a private right of action enabling individuals to sue for treble damages and attorney's fees.

Requires courts to order violators to cease and desist, divest pharmacies, disgorge prescription drug revenues received during the violation, and place disgorged funds into an FTC-administered community health fund.
Subjects any required divestment to mandatory reporting and review by the FTC and DOJ under antitrust laws, regardless of standard financial thresholds.
Directs the FTC to issue rules to carry out the section and requires quarterly compliance and status reports to congressional committees.

Exact names of specific corporations targeted, beyond general definitions of PBMs and health conglomerates.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 8779, known as the Patients Before Monopolies Act or the PBM Act, prohibits any entity from maintaining common ownership of both a pharmacy and an insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager (PBM). It requires companies that currently share such ownership to divest their pharmacy businesses within one year, provides enforcement mechanisms for federal and state authorities as well as private citizens, and grants antitrust agencies oversight and rulemaking powers.
summary_detail.significance: The bill structurally reorganizes the pharmaceutical supply chain and health insurance market by banning the vertical integration of pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacies. It establishes strict federal and state enforcement mechanisms, including mandatory divestment, profit escrow, disgorgement of revenue, and private lawsuits, impacting major national health conglomerates and the entire domestic pharmacy market.
